title: Ezekiel 40:1–16
context: In the twenty-fifth year of the exile, fourteen years after Jerusalem fell, the LORD's hand comes on the prophet again and brings him in visions of God to a very high mountain in the land of Israel. There a man whose appearance is like bronze, holding a flax line and a measuring reed, tells the prophet, whom he addresses as “Son of man,” to watch, listen, and declare everything to the house of Israel. The man begins measuring the outer wall and the east gate, with its rooms, posts, and porch. This begins the long temple vision of chapters 40–48. Readers in both traditions take it in different ways: as a plan for a literal future temple, as a symbolic or ideal picture of God dwelling with his people, or as fulfilled in Christ and the church. Ezekiel 43:10 gives one stated purpose: to show the house to Israel “that they may be ashamed of their iniquities.”

verses.text: In the twenty-fifth year of our captivity, in the beginning of the year, in the tenth day of the month, in the fourteenth year after the city was struck, in the same day, the LORD’s hand was on me, and he brought me there.
verses.arminianNotes: “In the twenty-fifth year of our captivity.” Arminian readers note the careful date, “in the fourteenth year after the city was struck,” which places the vision long after the news of Jerusalem's fall in 33:21.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that “the LORD’s hand was on me” echoes the opening of the book in 1:3. A priest in exile, far from any temple, is shown a new house of God. Both traditions treat the date as historical anchoring.

verses.text: In the visions of God he brought me into the land of Israel, and set me down on a very high mountain, on which was something like the frame of a city to the south.
verses.arminianNotes: “In the visions of God he brought me into the land of Israel.” Arminian readers see the same kind of visionary journey as in 8:3, when the prophet was brought “in the visions of God to Jerusalem.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the “very high mountain” and the “frame of a city.” Many compare Isaiah 2:2, where the LORD's house is raised above the hills, while others take the mountain more literally. Both traditions hold more than one reading.

verses.text: He brought me there; and, behold, there was a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze, with a line of flax in his hand and a measuring reed; and he stood in the gate.
verses.arminianNotes: “there was a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze.” Arminian readers see a heavenly guide sent to show the prophet the vision, equipped with a line and “a measuring reed.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the man is not named. Some readers take him as an angel, and others leave his identity open. Zechariah 2:1 and Revelation 11:1 also picture measuring as a sign of God's claim and care.

verses.text: The man said to me, “Son of man, see with your eyes, and hear with your ears, and set your heart on all that I will show you; for you have been brought here so that I may show them to you. Declare all that you see to the house of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Son of man, see with your eyes, and hear with your ears.” Arminian readers see the guide calling for full attention, because the prophet must “Declare all that you see to the house of Israel.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the vision is given to be passed on. As in Ezekiel 43:10–11, the details are meant to shape Israel's response, a purpose both traditions share.

verses.text: Behold, there was a wall on the outside of the house all around, and in the man’s hand a measuring reed six cubits long, of a cubit and a hand width each. So he measured the thickness of the building, one reed; and the height, one reed.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, there was a wall on the outside of the house all around.” Arminian readers see the wall marking off the holy area, with the man measuring it by a reed “six cubits long.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that each cubit is “a cubit and a hand width,” a longer measure than usual. The wall's thickness and height are both one reed. Many see the wall as a picture of separating the holy from the common, as 42:20 later says.

verses.text: Then he came to the gate which looks toward the east, and went up its steps. He measured the threshold of the gate, one reed wide; and the other threshold, one reed wide.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then he came to the gate which looks toward the east.” Arminian readers note that the tour begins at the east gate, the direction from which the LORD's glory will return in 43:2.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the glory had left the city toward the east in 11:23. Beginning at the east gate prepares for the glory's return, a link readers in both traditions often draw.

verses.text: Every lodge was one reed long and one reed wide. Between the lodges was five cubits. The threshold of the gate by the porch of the gate toward the house was one reed.
verses.arminianNotes: “Every lodge was one reed long and one reed wide.” Arminian readers see guard rooms lining the gateway passage, each the same size, with “five cubits” between them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the orderly, repeated measures. Whatever view one takes of the vision as a whole, the symmetry conveys a carefully guarded and well-ordered approach to God's house.

verses.text: He measured also the porch of the gate toward the house, one reed.
verses.arminianNotes: “He measured also the porch of the gate toward the house, one reed.” Arminian readers see the guide moving through the gateway step by step, measuring each part toward the inner area.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the brief verse belongs to a steady sequence of measurements. Readers have long found the exact layout of the gate hard to reconstruct from the text, and hold reconstructions loosely.

verses.text: Then he measured the porch of the gate, eight cubits; and its posts, two cubits; and the porch of the gate was toward the house.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then he measured the porch of the gate, eight cubits.” Arminian readers see the gate's porch and its posts of “two cubits” measured as the inner end of the gateway.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the relation of verse 8 and verse 9 is not fully clear, since both mention the porch. Readers in both traditions treat the general picture as more important than resolving every detail.

verses.text: The side rooms of the gate eastward were three on this side, and three on that side. The three of them were of one measure. The posts had one measure on this side and on that side.
verses.arminianNotes: “The side rooms of the gate eastward were three on this side, and three on that side.” Arminian readers see a balanced gateway with matching rooms on each side, all “of one measure.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the matching measures are a theme of the whole vision. Many see in the symmetry a picture of order and holiness fitting the LORD's dwelling.

verses.text: He measured the width of the opening of the gate, ten cubits; and the length of the gate, thirteen cubits;
verses.arminianNotes: “He measured the width of the opening of the gate, ten cubits.” Arminian readers see the guide noting the entrance width and the gate's length of “thirteen cubits.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the numbers serve the vision's purpose of showing a real, measured structure. Those who read it literally and those who read it symbolically both take the measurements seriously.

verses.text: and a border before the lodges, one cubit on this side, and a border, one cubit on that side; and the side rooms, six cubits on this side, and six cubits on that side.
verses.arminianNotes: “and a border before the lodges, one cubit on this side.” Arminian readers see a low barrier in front of the guard rooms and the rooms themselves measured at “six cubits” on each side.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that such details show the care with which the approach to God's house is laid out. The measurements are precise, though their full layout remains debated.

verses.text: He measured the gate from the roof of the one side room to the roof of the other, a width of twenty-five cubits, door against door.
verses.arminianNotes: “He measured the gate from the roof of the one side room to the roof of the other.” Arminian readers see the overall width of the gate, “twenty-five cubits, door against door.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this width will be repeated for the other gates in the vision. The repetition helps readers see that every gate shares one pattern.

verses.text: He also made posts, sixty cubits; and the court reached to the posts, around the gate.
verses.arminianNotes: “He also made posts, sixty cubits.” Arminian readers note that this verse is difficult, and readers differ on what the sixty cubits measure. The general sense is that the court reaches to the gate's posts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the difficulty and avoid building on any one reconstruction. The verse continues the description of the gate and its relation to the court around it.

verses.text: From the forefront of the gate at the entrance to the forefront of the inner porch of the gate were fifty cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: “From the forefront of the gate at the entrance to the forefront of the inner porch of the gate were fifty cubits.” Arminian readers see the full length of the gateway measured from end to end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this length of fifty cubits, with the width of twenty-five, will be repeated for the other gates. The repetition shows a common design throughout the courts.

verses.text: There were closed windows to the side rooms, and to their posts within the gate all around, and likewise to the arches. Windows were around inward. Palm trees were on each post.
verses.arminianNotes: “There were closed windows to the side rooms.” Arminian readers see windows lighting the gateway and its rooms, and “Palm trees were on each post” as decoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that palm trees also decorated Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:29). Many see in them a picture of life and flourishing, perhaps recalling Eden, though the text does not explain them.
